newsitem.title: USA: Critics say ATM surcharges threaten little banks.
newsitem.headline: Critics say ATM surcharges threaten little banks.

text.p: The Lake Wobegon bank may be in trouble soon, and the reason is those surcharges for using automatic teller machines.

Surcharges are a burgeoning source of revenue to big banks and other owners of ATMs, estimated to be worth $1 billion this year and growing. But little banks, credits unions and thrifts fear the surcharges mean trouble.

"I represent the Minnesota banks of Lake Wobegon," said Allen Olson, president of the Independent Community Bankers of Minnesota, which comprises 300 small banks Olson metaphorically locates in the fictional town created by author and radio personality Garrison Keillor. Olson fears a few dominant banks in Minneapolis spell trouble for his members.
"We believe these large institutions will use the surcharge to ultimately drive customers away from other financial institutions," Olson, of Eagan, Minn., said of the newly imposed fee.
In Washington State, Department of Financial Institutions Director John Bley of Olympia said he feels the same and wants his legislature to slap a moratorium on ATM surcharges.
"This is one step worse than predatory pricing," argues Bley, referring to the prohibited practice in which a big firm chops prices below cost to compete unfairly with a small firm.

Bley said big banks impose surcharges of $1 to $1.50 for each ATM transaction. To avoid the new fees, customers of small banks move their accounts to the more convenient big banks. In effect, the banks raise prices to undercut their competitor.
Not so, said Georgetown University law professor Steve Salop, a strong proponent of the surcharges.
"The banking relationship is quite complex," he said in Washington, saying that two studies show "there is no evidence" of switching.
The blunt-spoken Olson disagreed. "That's preposterous," he said. "That's bullbleep."
Olso argued that the federal government should outlaw surcharges.
The cause has been taken up by Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, who has promised hearings on the issue.

"I think the government has a responsibility to keep people from getting these charges that can amount to hundreds of dollars a year," said D'Amato, who has introduced a bill prohibiting the surcharges. He said when virtually all banks impose surchages, "... then they have distorted the free market."
But Salop said ATMs are "cash vending machines" whose owners should charge what they wish, like proprietors of Coke or Pepsi machines.
So far they do, and the practice is lucrative.

Don Davis, editor of Bank Network News, published by Faulkner & Gray in Chicago, estimates surcharges will generate $1 billion this year. He calls that "pure, bottom-line profit. There is no additional cost for charging it."

The surcharge is on top of an "interchange" fee, often around 50 cents, levied for handling an electronic transaction from another bank. ATM networks once prohibited additional fees, but Salop helped end that.
As lawyer for a small Texas thrift, Salop argued that large-bank members of the regional Pulse ATM network fixed the surcharge price at zero. An arbitrator agreed.
Price-fixing is prohibited under the nation's premier antitrust law, the Sherman Act, so his decision set the stage for a potentially punitive private antitrust suit. The Pulse network backed down.
"We allowed these charges out of concern we would be in violation of the antitrust law," said Pulse President Stan Paur. "We could have been liable for treble damages."

Now Paur supports the fees he once fought, finding it generates business. He said 3 percent of customers on the Pulse system pay the fee 10 times a month or more, by themselves accounting for 20 percent of the surcharges.

David Balto, an attorney adviser to the chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, has written on the subject and quoted then-judge and now Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer from a 1984 case on doctors fees:
"The Congress that enacted the Sherman Act saw it as a way of protecting consumers against prices that were too high, not too low," he wrote in Kartell v. Blue Shield.
